questions.question: State what is meant by tailgating.
questions.modelAnswer: Following an authorised person through a secure/controlled door to gain entry without using your own credentials.
markPoints: 1 mark for following an authorised person through a secure door / gaining entry without authorisation

questions.question: Describe the difference between a DoS and a DDoS attack.
questions.modelAnswer: A DoS (Denial of Service) attack uses a single computer to flood a target system with traffic so it becomes unavailable. A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack uses many computers (a botnet) to flood the target at the same time, making it harder to block.
markPoints: DoS uses a single source/machine (1)
DDoS uses many sources/a botnet, making it harder to stop (1)

questions.question: Explain one way trusted computing can help secure a network against threats.
questions.modelAnswer: Trusted computing reduces the risk of cyber-attacks (1) because it provides an extra layer of protection / verification before access is granted, increasing security (1).
markPoints: A way trusted computing helps (1)
Linked expansion/justification, e.g. extra layer/verification increasing security (1)

questions.question: Explain the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup.
questions.modelAnswer: A full backup copies all selected data every time it runs (1). An incremental backup only copies the data that has changed since the last backup, making it faster and using less storage (1).
markPoints: Full backup copies all data (1)
Incremental copies only changes since the last backup (1)

questions.question: Describe one digital threat to an organisation's network and an appropriate countermeasure for it.
questions.modelAnswer: A phishing attack is a threat where an attacker sends a deceptive email pretending to be from a trusted source to trick staff into revealing login credentials. This could give the attacker access to the network. An appropriate countermeasure is regular staff security-awareness training so employees can recognise and report phishing emails, combined with email filtering to block suspicious messages.
markPoints: Identifies a valid digital threat (1)
Describes how the threat works/affects the network (1)
Identifies an appropriate countermeasure (1)
Explains how the countermeasure reduces the threat (1)

questions.question: Explain why MAC address filtering only provides medium-level security for a Wi-Fi network.
questions.modelAnswer: MAC address filtering only allows listed devices onto the network (1), but a MAC address can be spoofed (faked) by an attacker who copies an allowed address, so it should not be relied on alone (1).
markPoints: Only listed MAC addresses are allowed (1)
MAC addresses can be spoofed/copied, so security is limited (1)

questions.question: State two rights that individuals have over their personal data under GDPR.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: the right to access their own data; to be informed how it is used; to have data corrected, removed or restricted; to object to processing; to data portability; not to be subject to a solely automated decision.
markPoints: 1 mark per correct GDPR right (max 2)

questions.question: Describe how an SQL injection attack works.
questions.modelAnswer: An attacker enters malicious SQL code into an input field on a website, such as a login or search box (1). If the input is not properly validated or sanitised, the database executes this code as part of a query (1). This allows the attacker to view, change or delete data they should not have access to, such as user credentials (1).
markPoints: Malicious SQL entered into an input field (1)
Input not validated/sanitised so it runs as a query (1)
Attacker can read/alter/delete database data (1)

questions.question: Explain one method of preventing SQL injection.
questions.modelAnswer: Use input validation / parameterised queries (1) so that user input is treated only as data and cannot be executed as SQL commands, preventing malicious code from running (1).
markPoints: A valid prevention method, e.g. input validation/parameterised queries (1)
Explanation of how it stops the injection (1)

questions.question: A network diagram needs a device added to provide secure internet access. Identify the device and state where it should be connected.
questions.modelAnswer: A firewall (1), connected between the router/internet connection and the internal network (1).
markPoints: Firewall identified (1)
Connected to the router/between internet and internal network (1)

questions.question: Describe how a VPN allows a remote worker to connect securely to their organisation.
questions.modelAnswer: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between the remote worker's device and the organisation's network over the public internet (1). Data sent through this tunnel is encrypted, so if it is intercepted it cannot be read (1). This lets the worker access internal files and systems securely as if they were on-site (1).
markPoints: Creates a secure tunnel over the internet (1)
Data is encrypted so interception is useless (1)
Allows secure access to internal resources (1)

questions.question: When configuring a DHCP server, the administrator enters the default gateway address. State two other pieces of configuration information that must be entered.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: the range of available IP addresses; the lease length/time; reserved/fixed IP addresses; the server address.
markPoints: 1 mark per valid DHCP configuration item (max 2)

questions.question: Describe one method of attacking a network by exploiting DHCP.
questions.modelAnswer: An attacker sets up a rogue DHCP server on the network (1). Because DHCP has no built-in authentication, client devices may accept IP configuration from the rogue server instead of the legitimate one (1). The attacker can then supply a malicious default gateway/DNS, routing the victim's traffic through their machine to intercept or alter it (1).
markPoints: Sets up a rogue/fake DHCP server (1)
DHCP has no authentication so clients trust it (1)
Attacker redirects/intercepts traffic via malicious settings (1)

questions.question: Staff and guest Wi-Fi both connect to a single switch, which is a security risk. Describe how the network should be changed to reduce this risk.
questions.modelAnswer: The guest and staff traffic should be separated using network segmentation, for example by placing them on separate VLANs or separate switches (1). Guest Wi-Fi should only be given internet access and kept off the internal network (1). This stops guests reaching staff devices/data and limits the lateral movement of any attacker (1).
markPoints: Separate the networks (segmentation/VLANs/separate switch) (1)
Restrict guests to internet-only / off internal network (1)
Prevents access to internal resources / limits attack spread (1)

questions.question: Explain the difference between an intranet and an extranet.
questions.modelAnswer: An intranet is a private network accessible only to an organisation's own staff (1). An extranet extends controlled access to selected external parties such as suppliers or partners (1).
markPoints: Intranet = internal/staff only (1)
Extranet = controlled access for selected outsiders (1)

questions.question: Explain one vulnerability of a wireless access point (WAP).
questions.modelAnswer: A WAP broadcasts radio signals that pass outside the building/through walls (1), so an attacker in a public area could intercept traffic or attempt to connect to the network (1).
markPoints: A valid WAP vulnerability, e.g. signal reaches public areas (1)
Linked expansion of the risk it creates (1)

questions.question: A password policy already covers length, sharing and uniqueness. Give two other sections a password policy should contain.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: password expiry/minimum age; lockout after failed login attempts; deny list of common/weak passwords; rules on storage/use of password managers.
markPoints: 1 mark per valid additional password policy section (max 2)

questions.question: Explain one advantage of staff using a password manager.
questions.modelAnswer: A password manager lets staff use long, unique, random passwords for every account (1) without having to remember them, reducing the risk of weak or reused passwords being cracked (1).
markPoints: An advantage, e.g. allows strong unique passwords (1)
Linked benefit, e.g. reduces weak/reused passwords / cracking risk (1)

questions.question: Explain one disadvantage of staff using a password manager.
questions.modelAnswer: If the master password is compromised, an attacker gains access to ALL stored passwords at once (1), creating a single point of failure that could expose every account (1).
markPoints: A disadvantage, e.g. single point of failure (1)
Linked consequence, e.g. all accounts exposed if master password compromised (1)

questions.question: Describe the main stages of a cyber security incident response.
questions.modelAnswer: First, triage and escalation — the incident is assessed and the right people are alerted (1). Then the main response — analysis, containment to stop it spreading, mitigation and recovery of systems (1). Finally, the incident is reviewed, reported and closed so lessons can be learned (1).
markPoints: Triage/escalation/initial decisions (1)
Containment, mitigation and recovery (1)
Review, report and close (1)

questions.question: Explain why an investigator takes a physical image of an entire drive instead of a targeted image of specific files.
questions.modelAnswer: A physical image copies the entire drive including deleted, temporary and system files (1), so it captures more potential evidence that a targeted image of only specific files might miss (1).
markPoints: Physical image copies the whole drive (incl. deleted/hidden data) (1)
Captures more evidence / a targeted image could miss data (1)

questions.question: Describe the process for creating a forensic image of a device's drive.
questions.modelAnswer: Connect the drive using a write-blocker so the original data cannot be changed (1). Use forensic imaging software to copy the entire drive bit-for-bit to a secure storage device (1). Generate a hash/checksum of both the original and the copy to prove the image is identical and has not been altered (1).
markPoints: Use a write-blocker / prevent changes to the original (1)
Create a bit-for-bit copy with forensic software (1)
Generate a hash/checksum to verify integrity (1)

questions.question: Explain which type of log file is likely to contain evidence that a password manager has been compromised.
questions.modelAnswer: Security/authentication logs are most likely to contain the evidence (1) because they record login attempts and access events, which would show unusual or unauthorised access to the password manager (1).
markPoints: Identifies security/authentication/access log (1)
Explains it records logins/access showing the compromise (1)

questions.question: Explain why a seized mobile device should be placed in a Faraday bag.
questions.modelAnswer: A Faraday bag blocks all wireless signals to and from the device (1), preventing it from being remotely wiped or altered, which preserves the evidence stored on it (1).
markPoints: Blocks wireless signals (1)
Prevents remote wipe/tampering, preserving evidence (1)

questions.question: State two requirements for ensuring forensic evidence is reliable.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: no action should change data on the device; collection by a competent person; a full record/trail of all actions (chain of custody); documenting who is responsible for each decision.
markPoints: 1 mark per valid reliability requirement (max 2)
